question: m07
q: What rate are owner-occupiers actually paying on new variable loans, compared with the advertised rate?

transcript.answer:
In August 2026, owner-occupiers paid an average of **6.2%** on new variable loans. That's about **2.6 points below the advertised standard variable rate (8.77%)** and **0.6 points below the advertised discounted rate (6.80%)**. August is the latest month for actual rates; advertised rates go up to September 2026 and haven't changed since May.

**Owner-occupier variable rates (% a year)**

| Month | Advertised standard | Advertised discounted | Actually paid, new loans | Gap to standard | Gap to discounted |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Jun 2025 | 8.27 | 6.30 | 5.8 | 2.47 | 0.50 |
| Dec 2025 | 8.02 | 6.05 | 5.5 | 2.52 | 0.55 |
| Mar 2026 | 8.52 | 6.55 | 5.9 | 2.62 | 0.65 |
| Jun 2026 | 8.77 | 6.80 | 6.3 | 2.47 | 0.50 |
| Aug 2026 | 8.77 | 6.80 | 6.2 | 2.57 | 0.60 |
| Sep 2026 | 8.77 | 6.80 | not yet published | – | – |

**What this shows:**
- **Almost nobody pays the standard rate.** New borrowers have paid about 2.5 points less throughout the period, so the advertised standard rate is mostly a starting point that lenders discount from.
- **The discounted rate is the closer guide,** but new borrowers still get about 0.5–0.65 points more off. Those extra discounts are usually negotiated or depend on the borrower's loan-to-value ratio, loan size or a package deal.
- **Actual rates followed the 2026 rate rises, but less than fully.** Advertised rates went up 0.75 points between February and May 2026 (8.02% to 8.77% standard, 6.05% to 6.80% discounted). Over the same months, the average rate on new loans rose 0.7 points, from 5.5% to 6.2%. It peaked at 6.3% in June before easing back to 6.2% in July and August, which suggests lenders are competing on price for new borrowers.
- **Existing borrowers pay about the same.** The average variable rate on all outstanding owner-occupier loans was also 6.2% in August 2026, so new borrowers aren't getting a noticeably better deal right now.

The figures come from RBA tables F5 (advertised rates at banks) and F6 (average rates on new loans funded each month, all lenders). F6 is published to one decimal place, so the gaps are only accurate to about ±0.05 points.
